sizeReason: Lina has 12 hours over two days. A single-page to-do list fits a small plan and the free-only budget. Focus on adding, ticking off, deleting, and saving tasks in the browser while learning JavaScript. Due dates and dark mode can wait.

parts.summary: Build a calm, minimal to-do web page for one person on their laptop. Lina will practise JavaScript while making tasks survive reloads and browser restarts.
parts.details: Lina has 12 hours over this weekend, knows HTML/CSS and a little JavaScript, and will own all the work. Spending stays at zero. There are no outside rules and no AI features.

parts.summary: Day one: add, tick off, delete and save tasks. Due dates and dark mode wait until after the weekend.
parts.details: Done means: adding a non-empty task shows it in the list; ticking it visibly marks it complete; deleting it removes it; reloading and reopening the same browser keeps the list and completion states, with deleted tasks still gone. Keep the appearance simple to protect JavaScript learning time. By hour 6, show all four actions working, including saved tasks. Use hours 7–8 for checks and fixes, with four hours left for unexpected trouble. Due dates and dark mode add extra behaviour and styling, so neither belongs in this weekend’s work.

risks.risk: JavaScript takes longer than Lina expects.
risks.action: Lina checks progress after each small feature, keeps the page plain and uses the four-hour reserve for learning and fixes.

risks.risk: Tasks appear saved but disappear after reopening the browser.
risks.action: Lina tests reload and browser restart by hour 6, using the same browser and page location. Repeat after the final fixes.

risks.risk: Visual polish or optional features consume the weekend.
risks.action: Lina leaves due dates and dark mode for later and stops styling once the page is clear and usable.

checklist.answer: Make a personal laptop to-do page that remembers tasks, while Lina learns JavaScript.
Add, tick off, delete and save are needed on day one. Due dates and dark mode wait because they add work beyond the basic goal.
1 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 8 planned hours; add 4 reserve hours = 12. The reserve is 33% of available time, exceeding 30%.
At hour 6, show adding, ticking, deleting and saving in a plain working page.
Every task names Lina as its sole owner and has one work area.
Layout uses Lina’s HTML/CSS skills. JavaScript work comes in small steps, with time to learn; she owns every area.
There are no dependencies on other people. Build layout, task actions and saving in that order, then test them together.
Lina’s total allocation is exactly her 12 available hours, including four hours of reserve.
Finish this weekend, within two days. Reserve the final planned work and spare time for testing and fixes; a final testing week does not apply.
Lina watches JavaScript delays, failed saving and extra styling work. Check saving early and keep optional features out.
Use this short task list and two progress checks. No separate schedule or decisions log is needed.
The brief is feasible within the time and free-only budget. No requested idea needs rejection; optional features are already deferred.
Add: text appears as a task. Tick: completion is visible. Delete: task disappears. Save: reload and browser restart retain the resulting list and states.
Hour 6: working demonstration. Hour 8: acceptance checks pass. If progress slips, cut visual polish first and use the reserve; preserve all four must-haves.

parts.summary: Use HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with localStorage: the browser’s built-in storage. This is free and builds on Lina’s skills within the 12-hour weekend.
parts.details: Keep page structure in index.html, calm styling in style.css, task rules in tasks.js, and browser interaction in app.js. Save after every change. Use a small local file server so the page always has the same address; opening HTML files directly has unreliable storage behavior. Python 3 can serve these files without any Python programming. Allow two hours for setup and learning JavaScript events, arrays and saving data. No framework, account system or database server is needed. [Browser storage behavior](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/localStorage).

options.name: Plain JavaScript + localStorage
options.good: Free, little setup, and direct JavaScript practice.

options.fit: Meets all four must-haves for Lina’s laptop.

options.good: Keeps tasks in a database file that is easy to copy.
options.bad: Needs extra server code to connect the page to the database.

decisions.why: Lina already knows HTML/CSS and wants JavaScript practice. Browser storage meets the single-laptop requirement with the least code.

risks.risk: Clearing browser data or using private browsing loses tasks.
risks.action: Use a normal browser profile and the same address. Document a manual storage-copy backup.

risks.risk: Saving fails because storage is blocked or full.
risks.action: Catch save errors and show that changes are unsaved. Preserve unreadable saved data instead of silently replacing it.

tasks.title: Set up local serving and learn events, arrays and storage
Build pure task rules and basic checks
Connect controls, rendering, saving and loading
Check persistence and failures; document running and backup

checklist.answer: HTML/CSS are familiar; JavaScript is partly new. Budget two learning/setup hours within Lina’s 12 hours.
One page and browser storage meet the must-haves. Drop frameworks, database servers and separate front-end projects.

Local serving costs nothing: about five file requests per reload and no requests per task edit. Estimate 1,000 short tasks below 1 MB; localStorage allows about 5 MiB per site and fails when full or blocked. No hosting rows, sleep or bandwidth limits apply. [Limits](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Storage_API/Storage_quotas_and_eviction_criteria).
There are no outside rules. Both options can run free on the laptop.

Controls → task rules → updated task list
Task list → page display + browser storage
Browser storage → task list on startup

Store one JSON list—text representing records—with id, text and done fields. For manual backup, copy its storage value through browser developer tools into a text file; document restoring it. No automatic backup.
Update the page immediately after each click. No shared users, background checking or live connection is needed.
This is a small, single-user project; a scaling plan is unnecessary.
Task functions take a list and return a new list. Keep storage, ID generation and page changes in app.js so rules can be checked without a browser or network.
Keep files below about 400 lines. Reuse task rules and save/render helpers; comments explain traps rather than repeat code.

First prove add → close browser → reopen preserves a task. Then check ticking, deletion, blank input, text containing HTML, unreadable storage and failed saves; check pure rules with small assertions.

Document installing Python 3 if needed, then running `python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1` in the project folder (`py` on Windows). Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 every time; target under 15 minutes. [Server instructions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/http.server.html).
Browser storage is simpler than running a database and fits the two-day deadline.
The brief fits. Keep due dates and dark mode deferred as requested; architecture tasks use 7.5 hours, leaving 4.5 for layout and buffer.
No passwords, service keys or other application secrets are needed.
Keep only task text, an ID and completion status in the browser. Collect no identity details or analytics.

HTTP is restricted to this laptop through 127.0.0.1; there is no public traffic or server input endpoint. Check task and saved-data shapes in JavaScript, reject blank text, and display text using textContent.

sections.summary: Lina will build a calm to-do page for her laptop while practising JavaScript: 12 hours this weekend, free only, no AI and no outside rules.
Day one covers adding, ticking off, deleting and keeping tasks; due dates and dark mode wait until later.

Page and storage: choose plain JavaScript with localStorage, the browser’s built-in storage—free and familiar, but tied to one browser; SQLite, a database stored in a file, offers copyable data but needs extra server code beyond Lina’s weekend.
Plan 8 hours of work and keep 4 hours spare, exceeding a 30% buffer; keep task rules separate from page controls and saving, and serve the page at one fixed local address.
Protect learning time, check saved tasks early, and show saving failures clearly.
